catalog_quote: Mbahám is a stress language which differs from what Yip (2002:4) calls "typical stress languages" in that in Mbahám stress is lexically specified. One cannot predict which syllable of a word will be prominent. Stress is not sensible to vowel quality. Any of the five Mbahám vowels can be stressed in word final and non-final positions. Examples are given in (102). ... In Mbahám, stress is not attracted to one particular type of syllable, nor is there a constant counting algorithm which determines its position. In Mbahám, stress is not sensitive to syllable weight or word boundaries. Quasi-minimal pairs are presented in (103). new_statements.quote: Mbahám is a stress language which differs from what Yip (2002:4) calls "typical stress languages" in that in Mbahám stress is lexically specified. One cannot predict which syllable of a word will be prominent. Stress is not sensible to vowel quality. Any of the five Mbahám vowels can be stressed in word final and non-final positions. [...] In Mbahám, stress is not attracted to one particular type of syllable, nor is there a constant counting algorithm which determines its position. In Mbahám, stress is not sensitive to syllable weight or word boundaries. Quasi-minimal pairs are presented in (103). [p. 96] [...] There is only one primary stressed syllable per word. In polysyllabic words, there may be a syllable carrying a secondary stress. Its position is predictable. It falls onto every alternate syllable before or after the stressed syllable. [p. 97]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (316 pp., existing text layer; text dump). Locator verified with extracted text: PDF p. 113 carries printed page number 96 and begins '4. Prosody.. 4.1. Stress'; PDF p. 114 carries printed 97 and begins 'Mbahám speakers generally do not mark stress.. There is only one primary stressed syllable per word.' The quoted passage is there word for word: 'Mbahám is a stress language which differs from what Yip (2002:4) calls "typical stress languages" in that in Mbahám stress is lexically specified. One cannot predict which syllable of a word will be prominent. Stress is not sensible to vowel quality. Any of the five Mbahám vowels can be stressed in word final and non-final positions.'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is a lexical property of each word and cannot be predicted from syllable weight, vowel quality, word edges, or a counting rule; it may fall on any syllable, final or non-final (quasi-minimal pairs /atáp/ 'string bag' vs /átak/ 'mud', /áni/ 'older brother' vs /ahí/ 'life'). One primary stress per word; secondary stress is rhythmic on alternate syllables away from the primary. Austronesian loans lean penultimate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, predictable: 'It falls onto every alternate syllable before or after the stressed syllable' (p. 97), e.g. /samará/ [sà.ma.rá], /méhawan/ [mé.ha.wàn], /tambú-tambu/ [tam.bú.dam.bù], /tambambíri/ [tàm.bam.bí.ri].
new_statements.exceptions: Austronesian loanwords tend to have penultimate stress (p. 97: 'Mbahám words borrowed from local Austronesian languages tend to have stress on the penultimate syllable'). Stress not sensitive to vowel quality, syllable weight, or word boundaries; unstressed vowels may delete in some contexts but stressed and secondarily stressed vowels cannot.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: 'There is only one primary stressed syllable per word' (p. 97). Compounds: 'In compound words, stress placement is not predictable. It surfaces on the first or second morpheme' (§3.2.1, p. 87). Pitch is partly decoupled from stress: an unsuffixed word has high F0 on the stressed syllable, but when a suffix is attached the high F0 shifts to the suffix regardless of stem stress (§4.2, p. 98), and in connected speech high F0 can land on final syllables of other words (p. 99). Stress correlates: loudness, duration, vowel quality, and pitch 'to a certain extent'; immediately pretonic vowels are phonologically and phonetically reduced (Ch. 3). Data are from the northern dialect (Flassy's 'variant B').
new_statements.identity_note: Cottet 2015 calls the language Mbahám (= Baham, bdw, baha1258; Glottolog lists no dialect glottocodes). Her stress statement rests on the northern dialect (Kokas district interior, = Flassy's 'variant B'); she explicitly excluded southern-dialect speakers from her corpus and reports only lexical differences between the two. Flassy et al. 1987 describe the southern-coast (Sanggram) variety.

sources.note: Ch.2 §4.1 'Stress' (pp. 96-97): Mbahám is a stress language in which stress is lexically specified and unpredictable; not sensitive to vowel quality, syllable weight, word boundaries, or any counting algorithm; one primary stress per word; secondary stress predictable on alternate syllables; Austronesian loans tend to penultimate; §3.2.1 (p. 87): in compounds stress falls unpredictably on first or second morpheme; §4.2 (pp. 98-102): high F0 on the stressed syllable shifts to a suffix when one is attached.
No dialect subdivisions listed; alternative name Patimuni; nothing on stress.
